Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Shepherd/.claude/skills/extract-from-conversations

# Extract lessons from a conversation

The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch

Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:

- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.

The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

1	# Extracting lessons — the bar and the local promotion ladder
2	
3	> **Scope: what both extraction skills share.** This doc is the **bar** a lesson must clear and the
4	> **ladder** it descends once it clears it — the half that is identical whatever the lesson was mined
5	> from. What each *source* adds is owned by its own skill:
6	> [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) for commits, merged PRs and issue
7	> activity, and [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) for a session's
8	> dialogue. Both load this doc; neither restates it.
9	
10	Its callers are the growth pack's [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md) daily task, which runs
11	both skills over one window, and an owner's occasional plain-words ask for a retrospective.
12	
13	## Run the pass on a capable model
14	
15	Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails
16	silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong "lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
17	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model to the judgment it
18	must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the separate efficiency analysis — also
19	live there; this doc is the how-to.
20	
21	## From signal to lesson — the bar
22	
23	A signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one
24	session or window.** Before adding anything:
25	
26	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded differently,
27	  even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
28	- **A dedupe miss has a second reading**, and when the candidate rule names an identifier you don't
29	  own — a function, field or setting — it is the likelier one: grep that identifier in the
30	  dependency's **code** before landing anything. No hit usually means the mechanism was retired and
31	  the rule is *expired*, not that the lesson is novel.
32	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or something already
33	  implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
34	- **Never capture a rule that teaches routing around a permission, security, or classifier denial.** A
35	  pattern of "it was denied, then succeeded on retry" is real signal about *reliability*, not license to
36	  write a rule instructing every future session to retry, ignore, or explain past such a denial without
37	  asking — however solid the retry evidence looks, that shape of lesson never clears the bar. Report a
38	  recurring denial to the owner instead; a checked-in instruction that tells unattended sessions to bypass
39	  a safety gate is a standing bypass with no consent behind it, however it got there.
40	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared, cross-project
41	  canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote stage lifts it there
42	  centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever travels.
43	
44	## Route to the local pack that owns it — the promotion ladder
45	
46	A project's capture surface is its **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/`); everything else
47	under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mounted canon and is never a capture target. Pick the pack whose
48	territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then
49	prefer the strongest mechanism it allows:
50	
51	**First check whether a canon pack already owns it, from the catalog and not from the mount.** A repo
52	holds only the packs it *declares*, so "nothing here covers this" is a fact about the mount rather than
53	about the corpus — and acting on it homes the lesson locally in territory a canon pack already owns.
54	Read `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md` (canon-side `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`),
55	which states every canon pack's boundary including the ones this repo doesn't hold. Where the owning
56	pack's stated territory is merely too narrow, propose widening it rather than routing around it.
57	
58	1. **A declared check** — an entry in that pack's `declared-checks.json`, whose `failureMessage` *is* the
59	   lesson. Nothing wires it: writing the declaration adds the check. This is the first rung to try for any
60	   lesson whose whole logic is "these patterns over these files", and most captured conditions are.
61	2. **A custom code rule** — a `<rule>.mjs` exporting `run(ctx)`, listed on the pack's `pack.mjs` — only
62	   when the check needs what patterns can't say: real parsing, structured-data field logic, git/diff or
63	   conversation state, a derived comparison. Reaching for code where a declaration would do costs a module
64	   to read and maintain for nothing.
65	3. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure rather than a condition.
66	4. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — the fallback, only what none of the above can carry.
67	
68	Either check rung ships with a **red-first fixture**; the declaration vocabulary is documented in
69	[`pattern-rules.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs)'s header, and the authoring shape for
70	both rungs in [`engine/checks/README.md`](../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule).
71	
72	Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
73	relocates it. When no pack's scope fits, the lesson lands in the repo's general local pack. A **new** local
74	pack is justified only by the repo's own **project structure** — a segment of the repo's tree whose work is
75	its own territory (a `client` pack for work under `client/`), so a repo's local packs mirror its layout.
76	**Never mint a local pack around a technology or a methodology**, however real the knowledge: capture those
77	lessons in the structural pack that owns the work, and let the canon-side promote stage — Claudinite's call,
78	never a member's — decide whether a technology or methodology facet earns a pack of its own.
79	
80	**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all.** A trap from misusing a specific API, class, or
81	library goes as a **comment right at the usage site** — next to the call itself, where the next editor of
82	that line sees it — never collected into a centralized gotchas list. Co-locate it in a file's own header
83	comment when the trap spans the whole file and you'd only hit it *while editing that file*. Reserve a
84	central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
85	file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.
86	
87	**Two kinds never become a pack rule, however strong the evidence** — filter on what the lesson is *about*
88	before picking a mechanism. (1) **The owner's own preferences** — which word authorizes a merge, tone, how a
89	summary is shaped. They belong to the person, are injected per session from their own preference file, and
90	change without any repo hearing about it; a pack copy goes stale silently and then contradicts the live one.
91	(2) **The agent framework's own loading mechanics** — which packs are declared, why a skill didn't mount, why
92	an injection missed. That's engine plumbing, not project knowledge: a real defect there is filed upstream, and
93	writing it down as a project rule preserves the bug instead of fixing it.
94	
95	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
96	
97	Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
98	nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
99	canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
100	reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.
101

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. # Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.

1	# Extracting lessons — the bar and the local promotion ladder
2	
3	> **Scope: what both extraction skills share.** This doc is the **bar** a lesson must clear and the
4	> **ladder** it descends once it clears it — the half that is identical whatever the lesson was mined
5	> from. What each *source* adds is owned by its own skill:
6	> [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) for commits, merged PRs and issue
7	> activity, and [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) for a session's
8	> dialogue. Both load this doc; neither restates it.
9	
10	Its callers are the growth pack's [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md) daily task, which runs
11	both skills over one window, and an owner's occasional plain-words ask for a retrospective.
12	
13	## Run the pass on a capable model
14	
15	Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails
16	silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong "lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
17	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model to the judgment it
18	must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the separate efficiency analysis — also
19	live there; this doc is the how-to.
20	
21	## From signal to lesson — the bar
22	
23	A signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one
24	session or window.** Before adding anything:
25	
26	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded differently,
27	  even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
28	- **A dedupe miss has a second reading**, and when the candidate rule names an identifier you don't
29	  own — a function, field or setting — it is the likelier one: grep that identifier in the
30	  dependency's **code** before landing anything. No hit usually means the mechanism was retired and
31	  the rule is *expired*, not that the lesson is novel.
32	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or something already
33	  implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
34	- **Never capture a rule that teaches routing around a permission, security, or classifier denial.** A
35	  pattern of "it was denied, then succeeded on retry" is real signal about *reliability*, not license to
36	  write a rule instructing every future session to retry, ignore, or explain past such a denial without
37	  asking — however solid the retry evidence looks, that shape of lesson never clears the bar. Report a
38	  recurring denial to the owner instead; a checked-in instruction that tells unattended sessions to bypass
39	  a safety gate is a standing bypass with no consent behind it, however it got there.
40	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared, cross-project
41	  canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote stage lifts it there
42	  centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever travels.
43	
44	## Route to the local pack that owns it — the promotion ladder
45	
46	A project's capture surface is its **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/`); everything else
47	under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mounted canon and is never a capture target. Pick the pack whose
48	territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then
49	prefer the strongest mechanism it allows:
50	
51	**First check whether a canon pack already owns it, from the catalog and not from the mount.** A repo
52	holds only the packs it *declares*, so "nothing here covers this" is a fact about the mount rather than
53	about the corpus — and acting on it homes the lesson locally in territory a canon pack already owns.
54	Read `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md` (canon-side `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`),
55	which states every canon pack's boundary including the ones this repo doesn't hold. Where the owning
56	pack's stated territory is merely too narrow, propose widening it rather than routing around it.
57	
58	1. **A declared check** — an entry in that pack's `declared-checks.json`, whose `failureMessage` *is* the
59	   lesson. Nothing wires it: writing the declaration adds the check. This is the first rung to try for any
60	   lesson whose whole logic is "these patterns over these files", and most captured conditions are.
61	2. **A custom code rule** — a `<rule>.mjs` exporting `run(ctx)`, listed on the pack's `pack.mjs` — only
62	   when the check needs what patterns can't say: real parsing, structured-data field logic, git/diff or
63	   conversation state, a derived comparison. Reaching for code where a declaration would do costs a module
64	   to read and maintain for nothing.
65	3. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure rather than a condition.
66	4. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — the fallback, only what none of the above can carry.
67	
68	Either check rung ships with a **red-first fixture**; the declaration vocabulary is documented in
69	[`pattern-rules.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs)'s header, and the authoring shape for
70	both rungs in [`engine/checks/README.md`](../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule).
71	
72	Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
73	relocates it. When no pack's scope fits, the lesson lands in the repo's general local pack. A **new** local
74	pack is justified only by the repo's own **project structure** — a segment of the repo's tree whose work is
75	its own territory (a `client` pack for work under `client/`), so a repo's local packs mirror its layout.
76	**Never mint a local pack around a technology or a methodology**, however real the knowledge: capture those
77	lessons in the structural pack that owns the work, and let the canon-side promote stage — Claudinite's call,
78	never a member's — decide whether a technology or methodology facet earns a pack of its own.
79	
80	**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all.** A trap from misusing a specific API, class, or
81	library goes as a **comment right at the usage site** — next to the call itself, where the next editor of
82	that line sees it — never collected into a centralized gotchas list. Co-locate it in a file's own header
83	comment when the trap spans the whole file and you'd only hit it *while editing that file*. Reserve a
84	central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
85	file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.
86	
87	**Two kinds never become a pack rule, however strong the evidence** — filter on what the lesson is *about*
88	before picking a mechanism. (1) **The owner's own preferences** — which word authorizes a merge, tone, how a
89	summary is shaped. They belong to the person, are injected per session from their own preference file, and
90	change without any repo hearing about it; a pack copy goes stale silently and then contradicts the live one.
91	(2) **The agent framework's own loading mechanics** — which packs are declared, why a skill didn't mount, why
92	an injection missed. That's engine plumbing, not project knowledge: a real defect there is filed upstream, and
93	writing it down as a project rule preserves the bug instead of fixing it.
94	
95	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
96	
97	Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
98	nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
99	canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
100	reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.

3	description: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.

5	
6	# Extract lessons from a conversation
7	
8	The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
9	taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
10	dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
11	what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.
12	
13	The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
14	surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
15	re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.
16	
17	## The goal
18	
19	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
20	waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
21	cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
22	a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.
23	
24	## Where the conversation comes from
25	
26	- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
27	  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
28	  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
29	  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
30	- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
31	  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.
32	
33	**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
34	when a session is done enough to mine.
35	
36	## What to look for — the friction signals
37	
38	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
39	necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
40	
41	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
42	
43	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
44	building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
45	answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
46	
47	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
48	user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
49	a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
50	the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
51	correctly **without the round-trip**.
52	
53	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
54	
55	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
56	that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
57	something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
58	convention and had it corrected in review.
59	
60	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
61	so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
62	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
63	first, not after a detour.
64	
65	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
66	
67	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
68	padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
69	hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.
70	
71	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
72	and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
73	(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
74	only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
75	was already optimal.
76	
77	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
78	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
79	the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
80	a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
81	loss of quality.
82	
83	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
84	
85	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
86	checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
87	fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
88	fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
89	relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
90	recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
91	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.
92	
93	## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch
94	
95	Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:
96	
97	- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
98	- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
99	  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
100	  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
101	  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.
102	
103	The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
104	stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
105	every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
106	breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.
107	
108	## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it
109	
110	For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
111	(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
112	nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):
113	
114	- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
115	- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
116	  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.
117	
118	**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
119	beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
120	**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
121	deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
122	silence it replaced.

## Summary of issue #269

Issue #269 was a `claudinite-dashboard/fleet-digest` work item: code-work had already ranked 59 candidate PRs/issues across the fleet into a 6-item shortlist on a data branch, and the agent's job was pure judgment — read the shortlist, pick the 4 strongest items, and write `digests/2026-08-24.md`. The session (04:54:43–04:58:53 UTC, ~4m10s total) read the task file and shortlist, wrote the digest in plain-text-safe format (per the `digest-plain-text` world-rule), ran `check_the_world.mjs`, opened PR #281, waited out CI, merged it, then manually converged work-item #269 (comment + label swap + close) after `converge-item.mjs` failed on `GITHUB_REPOSITORY is not set`.

## Friction found — none clears the bar

I found two friction signals, and both are **already covered** by existing rules, so I'm proposing no new lesson:

1. **`converge-item.mjs` dead end, again.** At 04:57:31–04:57:32 the agent ran `node .../queue/converge-item.mjs --issue 269 ...`, got `Exit code 1 / converge-item: GITHUB_REPOSITORY is not set`, then spent ~65s (04:57:37–04:58:38) reading `run-record.mjs`, `work-item.mjs` (twice, different offsets), `apply-status.mjs`, and grepping for `spellingsOf`/`STATUS_RUNNING_AGENT` to reconstruct the manual comment/label-swap/close sequence — before finally posting the `claudinite-task-exec v1 claudinite-dashboard/fleet-digest [#269] success` comment and closing the issue. This is exactly the dead end `RULES.md` already documents under "Reaching step 6 of a work-item run" (evidenced there by #126, #130, #133, #166, #202) — the rule already spells out the exact comment format, label swap, and close condition to use instead of the script. This session didn't retry the script (unlike #202), but it still re-derived the already-written manual procedure from source rather than applying it directly, costing ~65s. Since the rule already exists and already covers this failure mode, I'm not proposing a new entry — just flagging that this is a sixth live instance, which the rule's maintainer may want to fold in as evidence (I did not edit any file, per instructions).

2. **Re-running a check to recover its exit code.** At 04:56:26 the agent ran `check_the_world.mjs 2>&1 | tail -60`, got no output back (silently discarding the real exit code behind `tail`), then re-ran the identical check unpiped just to capture `$?`. This is precisely the anti-pattern basics/RULES.md already warns about ("Piping a long command's output through tail... discards the pipeline's real exit code... redirect to a file instead, read `$?` from that same invocation"). Already covered, cost was trivial (~3s), not worth a new rule — just evidence the existing rule wasn't applied even though it's loaded in every session's context.

No misunderstandings, corrections, or `AskUserQuestion` round-trips occurred — this was a fully unattended routine-fired session with no human turns. Everything else (delivery-preference lookup, digest plain-text formatting, PR creation, CI polling, `Blocked-by` sweep) followed existing documented procedure correctly with no backtracking.

## Wall-time measurements

- **Total session:** 04:54:43.004Z → 04:58:53.114Z ≈ **4m10s**, almost entirely compute (tool calls), essentially no idle time.
- **CI wait:** check started `in_progress` at 04:57:01Z, agent slept 12s (04:57:04→04:57:16), then polled and found it `completed` (`completed_at: 04:57:10Z`). So the check was actually done ~6s before the poll checked it — a single fixed `sleep 12` against a documented ~7–15s CI window is already close to optimal; a short-loop poll (e.g., 3–5s intervals) would have saved only ~5–6s. Not worth a new rule; consistent with the existing "poll in a short loop" guidance, just not maximally tight this once.
- **Manual converge reconstruction:** ~65s (04:57:32.959Z failure → 04:58:38.134Z comment posted) of file reads/greps that the existing rule's own written procedure could have skipped entirely.

**Conclusion: no new durable lesson from this log.** Both frictions found are already covered by standing rules (shepherd/RULES.md's `converge-item.mjs` entry, and basics/RULES.md's tail-discards-exit-code entry); this session is additional evidence for the first, not a new capture-worthy pattern. Per the skill's provenance rule, since nothing lands, no issue comment is posted.

## Summary of issue #273's session

Issue #273 was itself a Claudinite `growth-extract` run — the task that mines lessons and writes them into `.claudinite/local/packs/shepherd/`. The session did both halves in one run: the activity-half (reviewing 5 commits, 2 PRs, 6 issues) and the conversation-half, which fanned out 7 background subagents to mine one fresh conversation log (issue #246) plus a 6-log hindsight window (issues #2, #22, #24, #28, #30, #32). It verified the subagents' candidates, landed exactly one new rule (the "resume, don't redispatch, a flawed background subagent" rule, sourced from issue #246 and already recorded in `VERSIONS.md`/`RULES.md`), opened PR #282, merged it, and closed #273 — all in about 11.5 minutes wall-clock.

## Friction signals found — neither clears the bar

**1. Stray `TaskCreate` misuse (trivial, self-corrected).** At 04:52:25.612Z the orchestrator called `TaskCreate({subagent_type: "general", prompt: "placeholder"})` — the wrong tool shape entirely (missing `subject`/`description`, extra `subagent_type`/`prompt`, which belong to `Agent`). It failed instantly with `InputValidationError` and the very next tool call (Bash, 04:52:28) moved on correctly with no retry loop. Cost: one wasted call, ~2 seconds. This is a one-off tool-selection slip with no recurrence in the log and no generalizable fix beyond "know the tool schema" — below the bar (one-off, not reusable).

**2. Orchestrator re-mined sources it had just delegated — but this is a *recurrence*, not a new lesson.** After dispatching all 7 background subagents (04:55:05–04:55:44Z, each fired within a ~40s window — good parallel practice), the orchestrator spent the entire ~5.5-minute wait running dozens of its own `python3`/Bash extractions directly against the *same* log files it had just handed to subagents (e.g., repeated parses of `issue-28`, `issue-24`, `issue-2`, and `issue-246`'s log at indices 260, 264, 290, 304, 306, 311, 319, 323, 328, 337, 339, 342, 352, 355, 356, 358, 371, 383, 392, 395, 401, 404, 407, 421, 422, 428, 433, 439, 445, 464, 467, 477, 483 — well over 30 redundant reads). This is precisely the pattern already captured in `RULES.md`: *"Dispatching background subagents that each fully own one source... don't also read or grep it yourself while waiting"* (#201, landed 2026-08-24 — one day before this session ran, so the rule was already in context and was not followed). Per the dedup bar, a lesson already covered — even when it recurs — is not a new lesson; writing the same rule again would not fix an adherence gap. I'm reporting this as a notable non-finding rather than proposing new text.

Both candidates fail the bar: #1 for being a trivial one-off, #2 for being already covered verbatim by an existing rule.

## Measured wall-time waits

Dispatch → completion times for the 7 background subagents (from `Agent` call timestamp to matching `task-notification`):
- issue-30: 22.6s
- issue-24: 106s
- issue-22: 114s
- issue-32: 157s
- issue-28: 209s
- issue-2: 220s
- issue-246 (fresh pass, largest log): 331s (5.5 min) — this was the long pole gating the PR

Total session wall time: ~11.5 minutes (04:52:03Z start to 05:03:34Z session-end hook), of which ~5.5 minutes was the background-agent wait, bounded by the slowest single agent. The dispatch itself was already optimal — all 7 fired in parallel within a 40-second window, so there's no serialization to fix there. The only waste was *how* the orchestrator spent the wait (item #2 above): the redundant self-mining didn't lengthen wall-clock (it ran concurrently with the async background agents, gated by the slowest one regardless), but it burned tool calls/tokens for no benefit — exactly the cost the existing #201 rule was written to eliminate, and evidence that rule needs to actually be honored, not restated.

## Conclusion

No new lesson from this log clears the bar. Recommend no edit to `RULES.md`/`VERSIONS.md` from this pass.

1	# shepherd — this repo's own rules
2	
3	The capture surface for lessons **specific to this repository**. Loaded into every session
4	through the rules index, so what lands here should be a directive an agent can act on, not a
5	description of how something works.
6	
7	A lesson that would hold in another repo does not belong here — propose it to the Claudinite
8	canon instead, where every repo gets it.
9	
10	- **Reading this fleet's activity to rank or report it** — filter Claudinite's own artifacts out
11	  of **every** stream you collect, not just the first one you thought of. The machine is the
12	  busiest actor in this fleet, and its bookkeeping does not merely appear in a size-or-discussion
13	  ranking, it wins it: a dispatch issue collects a comment per executor stage, so it outweighs the
14	  work it dispatched, and a guard written for pull requests while issues go through unfiltered
15	  leaves the whole hole open. Recognize a machine artifact with the engine's own `isDispatchTitle`
16	  rather than a private regex, since the dispatch-title format is the scheduler's to change. Count
17	  the maintenance total where it is **tallied**, never by dropping items in the fetch: an issue the
18	  machinery filed and closed is still a true account of how much of the day this fleet spent
19	  servicing itself.
20	
21	- **Carrying an artifact directory over from a repo being retired** (the Sheepdog → Shepherd
22	  fleet-enforcer handoff) — verify the *machinery that produces it* came over too, not just its
23	  historical output. `digests/`'s files landed in #23 and read as fully carried; the missing
24	  generator (Sheepdog's `sheepdog-local` pack and its `fleet-digest` task) surfaced only later, in
25	  #27, once checked separately from the output. A copied output folder visually launders the
26	  absence of its live producer — audit for the generator explicitly, in the same pass, rather than
27	  inferring it from the presence of past output.
28	
29	- **Dropping a folded/aggregate `GENERATED` file because "the next run recomputes it"** — check
30	  first whether the recompute's own *inputs* retain the same history the current output does. A
31	  stateless recompute over inputs each fleet member keeps only for a bounded window starts the
32	  series shorter than a file carried over from elsewhere already holds — nearly true of
33	  `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json`, first left out of the Sheepdog carryover (#23) on exactly that
34	  assumption, then copied over verbatim once the gap was caught (#31). "The generator will refill
35	  it" is not sufficient on its own; confirm the generator's inputs cover the same span first.
36	
37	- **Scoping a fleet-wide text/reference sweep from this repo** — don't trust
38	  `mcp__github__search_code` alone to enumerate the affected member repos; its index can lag and
39	  silently undercount. Cross-check against the full known member roster (fetch each member's
40	  `.claudinite-checks.json` directly) before scoping the sweep: a Sheepdog-reference sweep found
41	  only 3 repos via search but 11 by direct check (#24).
42	
43	- **Renaming, adding, or removing a pack in `.claudinite-checks.json`** — re-run
44	  `node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/converge-wiring.mjs missingbulb/Shepherd --badges` in
45	  the same change. The README's `<!-- claudinite:packs -->` badge row is a one-time seed the
46	  update flow deliberately never re-derives, so it silently goes stale on every declaration
47	  change and only resurfaces later as a blocking `reference-integrity` finding — this exact gap
48	  hit twice, once for the `core`/`grow_with_claudinite` rename (#67, fixed in #69) and again for
49	  the `sheepdog` → `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog` rename (#79, fixed in #80/#81).
50	
51	- **Waiting on this repo's PR CI** — it's a single `checks` job that completes in roughly 7–15
52	  seconds (measured directly across #30, #32, #59, #67). Poll `pull_request_read get_check_runs`
53	  in a short loop instead of a fixed or backgrounded `sleep`, and don't call
54	  `enable_pr_auto_merge` in the same breath as opening the PR — GitHub refuses it with "unstable
55	  status" if the check hasn't started yet, which is a sign to wait and re-poll, not license to
56	  merge by hand instead (#59). Before stating a PR's status in a closing callout, read
57	  `get_check_runs` rather than asserting "CI running" as an unread guess (#30), and skip grepping
58	  `.github/workflows/*.yml` to guess whether a workflow gates the merge — the check runs already
59	  say so directly (#60).
60	
61	- **Firing an `AskUserQuestion`** — check first whether the answer is already decided: by a rule
62	  already loaded in context, by fleet or repo state one read away (a sibling's
63	  `.claudinite-checks.json`, a pending adoption interview), or by the option marked
64	  "(Recommended)" simply being the status quo. Batch every open decision a run will need into one
65	  question instead of asking serially. Four sessions lost 17 to 105 minutes of pure
66	  human-round-trip idle time to questions whose answer was already available or was the presented
67	  default (#2, #22, #28, #32).
68	
69	- **Leaving multiple PRs open for the owner after a fleet-wide sweep** — call
70	  `subscribe_pr_activity` on every one of them, not a sample. #24's sweep subscribed only 2 of 12
71	  open PRs, then spent over two hours and ~29 API calls re-polling the other 10 on a self-armed
72	  hourly wake-up with zero state change, while the 2 subscribed PRs' merges arrived instantly as
73	  activity events the moment the owner acted.
74	
75	- **Triaging a `fleet-drift` issue that names another repo** — don't spend a call on
76	  `mcp__github__get_file_contents` (or any other repo-scoped MCP read) against that repo: this
77	  session's GitHub access is scoped to `missingbulb/Shepherd` only, and every cross-repo call is
78	  denied outright. Five separate triage subagents each independently spent a call rediscovering
79	  that denial before falling back to the only place the answer actually lives — the issue body's
80	  own self-description of how the item converges (#104).
81	
82	- **Hunting for this repo's own standing tracker issue by its exact title** —
83	  `mcp__github__search_issues` with a quoted title and `in:title` does not reliably filter; it can
84	  return the same broad, unfiltered issue list regardless of the query text, burying the real
85	  tracker in a couple dozen unrelated hits (and once, overflowing the token cap entirely). The same
86	  unreliability hits `mcp__github__list_issues`'s `query` param too — one run got back an entirely
87	  unrelated issue for a quoted-title query even with `minimal_output: true` set (#210). And
88	  `minimal_output: true` alone doesn't bound the response either: another run overflowed the token
89	  cap with `minimal_output: true` set and no filter, on a real result set of just 3 issues
90	  (#209) — the label/state filter is the load-bearing part, not `minimal_output`. Scan the
91	  returned list for the exact title yourself, or narrow with `minimal_output: true` **plus** a
92	  label/state filter, rather than trusting the query text on either tool to do the narrowing
93	  (#104, #88, #209, #210).
94	
95	- **Pushing a change that touches `.github/workflows/`, `.claudinite-checks.json`, or pack
96	  config** — run `node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` locally first. It's
97	  the exact script the PR's `checks` CI job runs, and finding a `[BLOCKING]` finding live on the PR
98	  costs a full push-PR-CI-diagnose-fix-re-push round trip that one ~4-second local run skips
99	  (#106).
100	
101	- **Dispatching concurrent subagents that each `git show` a file into the shared scratchpad** (the
102	  conversation-extract fan-out, or any similar parallel mining pattern) — give every dispatch a
103	  unique output filename. A shared generic name (`log.jsonl`) collides across concurrent downloads
104	  and silently hands one agent another agent's bytes; this exact contamination hit a prior
105	  growth-extract run in six or more of its own subagents (#73) and recurred in this run's own
106	  fan-out before being caught and re-fetched to a uniquely-named path.
107	
108	- **Branching off this checkout's local `main`** — it does not track the live default branch, and
109	  has been observed pinned at the repo's very first commit. A plain `git checkout -b <name> main`
110	  silently branches from that frozen history and the next script that expects current content
111	  (e.g. a `.claudinite/` path) fails confusingly. Always `git fetch origin main` and branch from
112	  `origin/main` explicitly (#73).
113	
114	- **Reaching step 6 of a work-item run** (`node .../scheduler/queue/converge-item.mjs`) — it will
115	  fail here: the script's read/write path (`signals/gh.mjs`) is documented in its own header as
116	  Action-side only ("everything session-side stays MCP-only"), and this session's `GITHUB_TOKEN` is
117	  a proxy placeholder the REST API rejects outright ("GitHub access is not enabled for this
118	  session"), confirmed across attempts with `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` set, with `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`,
119	  and via raw `curl`. Don't re-diagnose it — go straight to replicating the transition by hand
120	  over the GitHub MCP tools: the execution-record comment in `run-record.mjs`'s exact format
121	  (`claudinite-task-exec v1 <pack>/<task> [#<n>] <status>`), the `task:agent`→outcome label swap,
122	  the close with the matching `state_reason`, and (what `readyDependents` would have released) a
123	  check for any open item naming `Blocked-by: #<n>`. Four independent sessions in one day each lost
124	  2–5 minutes rediscovering this same dead end (#126, #130, #133, #166); a fifth still ran the
125	  script itself twice — once without `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` set, once with — before switching to
126	  the manual path, costing ~77s despite this very rule already being loaded in context (#202):
